title: Here's How BP is Balancing Fossil Fuels & Renewables for Cleaner Air - The Globe and Mail
content: Air quality continues to deteriorate globally due to rising emissions from transportation, industrial activity and rapid urbanization, increasing risks to public health and the environment. In response to these challenges, governments and industries are prioritizing cleaner energy solutions by adopting low-emission fuels, stricter standards and sustainable technologies to support the global energy transition. BP plc BP is positioning itself for this transition by combining its traditional fossil fuels operations with expanding renewable energy and low-carbon businesses. BP has built a strong renewable portfolio, spanning solar, wind and bioenergy, by utilizing capital-light partnerships to reduce risk. The company continues to expand its solar and battery storage presence through partnerships such as Lightsource bp, while its JERA Nex bp joint venture strengthens its offshore wind platform. BP has also established a growing position in renewable natural gas through Archaea Energy, supporting cleaner fuel demand across transportation and energy-intensive industries. Beyond its renewable portfolio, BP is focusing on difficult-to-decarbonize sectors to help significantly lower atmospheric emissions. The company is advancing this goal by developing low-carbon hydrogen production facilities and large-scale carbon capture and storage (CCS) projects. Through these strategic partnerships and targeted investments, BP continues to strengthen its long-term energy transition strategy while supporting global efforts to lower emissions and improve air quality. Other leading integrated energy giants Chevron Corporation CVX and Exxon Mobil Corporation XOM are actively advancing initiatives to improve air quality. Chevron is reducing emissions by investing in carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS) technologies to trap carbon dioxide underground. CVX is increasing its production of renewable fuels, including biodiesel, renewable natural gas and hydrogen, to help reduce emissions. Like BP, ExxonMobil has established its own low carbon solutions business. Through this division, XOM is building large-scale CCS facilities along the U.S. Gulf Coast, a vital energy-producing corridor, to safely capture and isolate industrial emissions. BP shares have gained 42.7% over the past year compared with the 44.5% growth of the industry. From a valuation standpoint, BP trades at a trailing 12-month enterprise-value-to-EBITDA (EV/EBITDA) of 3.11X. This is below the broader industry average of 6.42X. title: Why analyst sees ExxonMobil stock outperforming the S&P500 in 2026 - TradingView
content: ExxonMobil (XOM) has surged ahead of the broader market this year, with analysts at The Motley Fool predicting the oil giant will continue to outperform the S&P 500. The forecast, published by The Motley Fool, comes as Exxon shares have already climbed 24% in 2026, compared with a 10% gain for the benchmark index. The rally underscores how energy majors are benefiting from geopolitical disruptions that have kept oil prices elevated. The analysis highlights that ExxonMobil’s gains are not simply a matter of investor sentiment but are rooted in real supply shortages. The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has disrupted oil flows, pushing Brent crude higher and boosting earnings prospects for integrated energy companies. “Exxon is benefiting from investor enthusiasm right now. Only, the excitement around the stock is tied to a very real-world event the geopolitical conflict in the Middle East,” Motley Fool contributor Reuben Gregg Brewer wrote. With the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed, millions of barrels of supply have been taken offline. For ExxonMobil, which has extensive upstream operations and refining capacity, the disruption translates into stronger margins and cash flow. Investors have rewarded the company’s ability to weather volatility, driving its stock well ahead of the S&P 500. ExxonMobil’s fundamentals also underpin the bullish outlook. The company has maintained a disciplined capital program, focusing on high-return projects while preserving its dividend a key attraction for long-term investors. Its integrated model, spanning exploration, production, refining, and chemicals, provides resilience against swings in crude prices. This structure allows Exxon to capture value across the energy chain, making it more robust than pure-play producers. Brewer noted that investor emotions often drive short-term moves, but in Exxon’s case, enthusiasm is grounded in fundamentals. The company’s dividend track record and capital discipline further strengthen investor confidence, making it a preferred choice for those seeking stability amid market turbulence. The report cautions that ExxonMobil’s rally is not without risks. If peace talks between the US and Iran succeed and oil prices retreat, ExxonMobil’s momentum could slow. Yet normalization of supply will take time, even under a framework agreement. Mines must be cleared, infrastructure repaired, and shipping restored before the market stabilizes. That lag gives ExxonMobil room to sustain its advantage in the months ahead. Brewer acknowledged that Exxon’s stock could decline once oil prices ease, but emphasized that the global oil market’s complexity means normalization may take months. Until then, ExxonMobil is positioned to continue benefiting from elevated benchmarks. The prediction that ExxonMobil will outperform the S&P 500 underscores the continued importance of energy stocks in diversified portfolios. While technology and growth sectors have dominated headlines, commodities remain a critical driver of returns during periods of geopolitical stress. For investors, ExxonMobil offers exposure to both the upside of elevated oil prices and the stability of a blue-chip dividend payer. Energy-driven inflation also complicates the Federal Reserve’s policy outlook. Higher oil prices could prompt further rate hikes, weighing on equities broadly. Yet for ExxonMobil, elevated crude remains a tailwind, reinforcing its relative strength against the wider market. Looking ahead, the trajectory of ExxonMobil’s stock will hinge on the pace of Middle East negotiations and the Fed’s response to inflation. Analysts expect the company to continue generating strong cash flow, supporting shareholder returns and reinforcing its market leadership. With shares already far outpacing the S&P 500, The Motley Fool believes ExxonMobil is positioned to extend its lead as the year unfolds. While risks remain tied to peace talks and eventual price normalization, ExxonMobil’s fundamentals and current momentum suggest it will continue to outperform the broader market. Oil companies routinely hedge their production to protect against price movements in energy markets. In this case, that hedging turned into a headwind. Oxy, which is much less exposed to the Middle East than Exxon or Chevron, was a relative standout. At the other extreme was Exxon, which has more exposure to the region and saw its production impacted. That said, its $1.16 per share in earnings beat the analyst call of $1.01. But hedging led to a $700 million earnings hit. That should be reversed in the second quarter as shipments hedged are delivered. Still, the short-term impact is worth noting as you examine the business. Chevron, meanwhile, fell between Exxon and Oxy, with its $1.41 per share earnings beating Wall Street's $0.97 per share call. But once again, the company's hedging activity was a headwind, as management took a $2.9 billion charge related to it. Hedging is company-specific, with each company adopting a different approach. And because hedging is a proprietary activity, investors won't know about the impact, good or bad, until the company releases quarterly results. That said, the refining operations of Exxon and Chevron performed weakly, with timing and hedging both playing a role. Oxy recently sold its downstream business at the start of 2026, so this business wasn't a meaningful issue for the company in the quarter. Simply put, there are a lot of moving parts to consider when you look at individual energy companies. In the end, Oxy, Exxon, and Chevron are all benefiting from rising energy prices, but the way they are playing the rise is slightly different. And that, in turn, is leading to different outcomes. title: Is Exxon Mobil's Recent Surge Sustainable Amid Middle East Tensions - Kavout
content: Exxon Mobil (XOM) stock has been a standout performer in recent weeks, with shares trading at $154.19 as of March 2, 2026, up 1.11% on the day and nearing its 52-week high of $159.35. This impressive run, which saw the stock climb from $115.15 on November 30, 2025, to $152.50 by March 1, 2026—a 32.4% increase—is largely attributed to a dramatic shift in the global energy landscape. The "Midnight Hammer" crisis in the Middle East, characterized by retaliatory strikes and a de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz, has injected a significant risk premium into crude oil markets. This geopolitical shock has sent oil prices soaring, with WTI crude currently at $71.15 per barrel, having recently spiked towards $73 and Brent crude briefly touching $100 per barrel. The Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for 20% of global seaborne oil, has seen shipping halted and war risk coverage cancelled by marine insurers, effectively stranding an estimated 15 million barrels per day (bpd) of global supply. This immediate supply disruption, combined with a perceived failure of OPEC+ to adequately increase production, has fueled a rapid "risk-off" rotation into hard assets like oil. The market's reaction on March 2, 2026, saw XOM and Occidental Petroleum (OXY) both climb 2.1% by midday, even as the broader S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite tumbled. This divergence underscores a fundamental reassessment of value in an uncertain geopolitical climate, where the "old economy" energy trade has become a defensive hedge. While the immediate catalyst is conflict, the underlying "AI Power Crunch"—the insatiable demand for energy to fuel massive data centers—is also contributing to a structural revaluation of energy companies. However, the sustainability of this surge hinges precariously on the resolution of the Strait of Hormuz standoff. Analysts warn that a diplomatic "off-ramp" within the next 72 hours could lead to a significant cooling of oil prices. Conversely, if the blockade persists, a "super-spike" toward $120 per barrel is possible, which would almost certainly tip the broader global economy into a recession by Q3 2026. This delicate balance means XOM's recent gains, while substantial, are tied to highly unpredictable global events. The current surge in oil prices provides a significant tailwind for Exxon Mobil's Q1 2026 earnings, potentially rewriting near-term cash flow math. Higher crude prices directly enhance the profitability of Exxon's Upstream segment, which saw a 41% increase in revenue in Q1 2025, including a remarkable 234% jump in its U.S. Upstream operations. This segment is particularly sensitive to commodity price fluctuations, making the current environment highly favorable for top-line growth and margin expansion. Despite a 6% decline in net profit and a 15% fall in EPS in Q1 2025 due to weaker refining margins and petrochemicals, the company demonstrated resilience later in the year. Exxon Mobil reported strong Q3 2025 earnings of $7.5 billion and $14.8 billion in cash flow, followed by a Q4 2025 EPS of $1.71, beating estimates. This consistent outperformance, marking the fourth consecutive quarter of earnings beats, suggests an underlying operational strength that can capitalize on improved market conditions. Analysts are already adjusting their expectations, with Bank of America raising ExxonMobil's price target from $135 to $151, reflecting confidence in enhanced future profitability due to the oil risk premium. The consensus Q1 2026 EPS is projected at approximately $1.53, a figure that could prove conservative if oil prices remain elevated throughout the quarter. Exxon's ability to generate substantial free cash flow, projected at $52 billion for the 2025-2026 period, further strengthens its financial position to navigate market dynamics. However, it's not a clear-cut picture. While Upstream benefits, the Energy Products (refining) and Chemical Products segments can face margin pressures. In Q1 2025, Energy Products revenue declined 4% and Chemical Products revenue fell 8%, largely due to falling refining margins and an oversupply in the global chemical market. Therefore, while high crude prices boost one side of the business, investors must monitor product solutions segment margins and overall production guidance during the Q1 2026 earnings call, expected in late April, to gauge the full impact. Beyond the immediate tailwinds from geopolitical tensions, Exxon Mobil's long-term investment thesis is underpinned by its strategic focus on "advantaged barrels" and robust production growth from key assets. The company's operations in Guyana, particularly the Stabroek block, are a cornerstone of this strategy. Projects like Uaru, expected to start up by year-end 2026 with a capacity of 250,000 b/d, and Whiptail, forecast to add another 250,000 b/d next year, are set to boost Guyana's daily oil production well beyond 1 million b/d. Exxon Mobil is also actively developing Guyana's significant recoverable gas resources, especially in the southeast part of the Stabroek block. The Hammerhead project, for instance, is designed to transport gas by pipeline to shore, complementing oil production. The company has already completed its first gas-to-energy pipeline, awaiting an onshore power plant to lower electricity costs in Guyana. This integrated approach to resource development highlights Exxon's commitment to maximizing value from its world-class geology and competitive development costs. The Permian Basin in the U.S. shale patch remains another critical growth engine. CEO Darren Woods has stated there is "no near-term peak Permian" for Exxon, citing over 40 technologies currently in testing to enhance recovery and efficiency. This focus on low-cost, high-margin production in both Guyana and the Permian has made XOM a "HALO" stock (Heavy-Asset, Low Obsolescence) for investors seeking stability and long-term value. Furthermore, Exxon Mobil's commitment to shareholder returns is a significant draw. The company has a strong track record of distributing capital through dividends and share repurchases, having distributed $9.4 billion in Q3 2025 and $9.5 billion in Q4 2025. As a dividend Aristocrat, boasting 26 consecutive annual dividend increases, XOM offers a compelling proposition for income-focused investors, signaling management's confidence in its ability to generate sustained free cash flow and maintain financial discipline. While Exxon Mobil benefits from current market dynamics, several significant risks could derail its long-term investment thesis. The most immediate concern remains commodity price volatility. Despite recent spikes, energy prices are inherently sensitive to geopolitical events, OPEC+ decisions, and global demand fluctuations. A sharp decline in prices, whether due to de-escalation in the Middle East, falling global demand, or oversupply, could significantly reduce ExxonMobil’s income, particularly in its highly profitable Upstream segment. Beyond oil prices, the company faces regulatory and political risks. Stricter environmental legislation globally, including potential bans on exploration in sensitive regions, new emissions standards, and tighter regulation of refining, could increase operating costs or limit production capacity. The accelerating global energy transition to lower-carbon sources poses a fundamental threat to long-term demand for fossil fuels, potentially diminishing Exxon Mobil's core product revenue streams and creating significant market risks. Exxon Mobil's diversified earnings are also susceptible to global chemical market oversupply and weak refining margins. As seen in Q1 2025, the chemical segment experienced substantial earnings reductions due to "bottom-of-cycle" margins. This cyclicality can act as a significant drag, even when other segments perform well. The capital-intensive nature of its upstream and downstream mix constrains revenue growth assumptions, keeping them modest at around 2.3%. Finally, valuation concerns persist among some analysts. With a TTM P/E ratio of 23.15 and a current price of $154.19, some models suggest the stock is trading at a premium. Analyst consensus price targets range around $140-$142, implying a modest downside from current levels. For instance, one model projects a $140.92 fair value, representing a 6% downside. While the company's beta of 0.35 reflects lower volatility than the broader market, a retreat in oil prices after tensions ease could expose valuation risks, making the stock less attractive at current levels. Navigating the current volatile energy market with Exxon Mobil requires a nuanced approach, balancing short-term tactical plays with long-term strategic considerations. For investors looking to capitalize on immediate geopolitical shocks, XOM's strong correlation with oil prices, coupled with its robust production and cash flow, makes it a compelling option. The stock's beta of 0.35 indicates lower volatility compared to the broader market, offering a degree of stability even in turbulent times. However, a purely short-term strategy is fraught with risk. The unpredictable nature of geopolitical events means any sudden de-escalation could lead to a sharp correction in oil prices and, consequently, in XOM's stock. Investors should consider XOM as a "HALO" stock, benefiting from heavy assets and low obsolescence, but remain vigilant. Monitoring key events like OPEC+ ministerial meetings for changes in production quotas, and geopolitical developments in critical regions like Guyana, is paramount. For long-term investors, Exxon Mobil's status as a dividend Aristocrat, with a current dividend yield of 2.6% and 26 consecutive annual increases, offers a compelling income component. This consistent return to shareholders, alongside disciplined capital allocation and share repurchase programs, provides a defensive moat against market fluctuations. The company's strategic investments in low-cost, high-return assets like the Permian and Guyana further solidify its long-term growth potential, irrespective of short-term price swings. To mitigate risks, diversification remains key. While XOM offers exposure to the energy sector, considering alternatives like ConocoPhillips (COP) for a more pure-play upstream focus, or Canadian Natural Resources (CNQ) for its strong inventory and capital discipline, could balance a portfolio. Ultimately, investors should maintain a conservative position sizing, perhaps 1% to 3% of their portfolio, given the stock's near-term volatility and the cyclical headwinds in its downstream and chemical segments. Exxon Mobil stands at a pivotal juncture, poised to benefit from current geopolitical tailwinds while navigating inherent industry volatility. Its strategic asset base and commitment to shareholder returns offer a compelling long-term narrative, but investors must remain acutely aware of the risks. Prudent portfolio management, informed by ongoing market developments, will be essential to capitalize on XOM's potential in this dynamic environment. Want deeper research on any stock? The Phase 3 expansion aims to significantly increase production from 60 thousand barrels per day (MBPD) to 150 MBPD, while gas output is expected to reach 200 million cubic feet per day (MMcf/d) from 80 MMcf/d. By continuing its phased and fast-track development model, Eni is expected to reach early production milestones and reduce costs by leveraging existing infrastructure. The integrated energy giant emphasized that all gas produced from the project will be supplied to Cote d’Ivoire’s domestic market to support electricity generation, industrial development and national energy security. title: USO, UCO, BATL, XOM Slip: Oil Dips Below $100 After Trump Says Iran Talks ‘Proceeding Nicely’ - Stocktwits
content: Major oil stocks and index funds declined in the overnight session heading into Tuesday after U.S. President Donald Trump said negotiations with Iran “are proceeding nicely,” pushing crude below $100 a barrel. Shares of the United States Oil Fund (USO) and ProShares Ultra Bloomberg Crude Oil ETF (UCO) slipped 4.7% and 5.4% lower, even as Battalion Oil (BATL) fell more than 6% in the overnight session at the time of writing. Exxon Mobil Corp. (XOM) fell more than 1%, while Trio Petroleum Corp. (TPET) and Indonesia Energy Corp Ltd. (INDO) shares lost more than 2% each. Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Monday that negotiations with Iran “are proceeding nicely!” but added, “It will only be a Great Deal for all or, no Deal at all — Back to the Battlefront and shooting, but bigger and stronger than ever before — And nobody wants that!” Oil futures were below $100 a barrel on hopes for a deal, with Brent crude futures expiring in July trading at around $98.12 a barrel at the time of writing, while WTI crude futures expiring in June slipped more than 5%, trading around $91.71 a barrel. The comments come amid reports of an Iranian delegation traveling to Qatar for consultations with senior officials to negotiate a deal with the U.S. to end the war. A report from Al Jazeera has noted that Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, and Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati are in Doha to discuss sticking points for the potential deal that could end the U.S.-Israel war on Iran. Trump had said earlier on Monday that an agreement with Iran must be “meaningful” for a deal to be reached. The president has insisted that Iran must give up its nuclear power for a deal, while Tehran has said that at this stage, Iran and the U.S. have not been “talking about the nuclear issue.” Reports have also indicated that the U.S. and Iran are discussing a plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz roughly 30 days after a deal is finalized, with Iran expected to remove mines from the waterway to ensure safe maritime passage, according to Nikkei. Meanwhile, the U.S. military carried out what it described as “self-defense strikes” in southern Iran, targeting Iranian missile installations and boats allegedly attempting to deploy mines in the strait. Robin Brooks, a Senior Fellow at The Brookings Institution and a former chief FX strategist and managing director at Goldman Sachs, thinks oil prices will normalize as the critical waterway opens. “It'll obviously take time for shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz to normalize, but don't fall into the trap of thinking this means oil prices will stay high. Markets are forward-looking, so they'll price normalization long before it happens…” he said in a post on X. Meanwhile, Mohamed El-Erian, Chief Economic Advisor at Allianz, noted oil’s slip below $100 a barrel, adding that prices would depend on peace deal negotiations and traffic flow through the strait. “Brent crude is now trading well below $100 a barrel. Where this crucial price goes next will depend not only on whether the agreement is finalized but also on the details and what they imply for sustainability—particularly with respect to the return of free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz,” he said in a post on X. However, Barclays has said that it expects Brent crude oil to be around $100 for 2026, while also warning that price risks are skewed higher. Meanwhile, the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) projects Brent crude prices to average about $106 per barrel in May and June, citing expectations that global oil inventories will decline by roughly 8.5 million barrels per day during the second quarter of 2026. The agency also said that increasing oil output from the Middle East is likely to push crude prices down to an average of $89 per barrel by the fourth quarter of 2026, with prices easing further to around $79 per barrel in 2027. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment toward USO, BATL, and XOM was in the ‘bearish’ territory, while UCO sentiment was in the ‘bullish’ territory at the time of writing. Message volumes were in the ‘high’ levels for UCO, while they were ‘normal’ for USO and XOM. Messages for BATL were ‘extremely low’ at the time of writing. One user said, “The price of oil is showing you that Iran has nothing. Last week was a chance to sell above 100. This week above 90. Soon, Brent will be under 90. There are very few real oil bulls left in this market, it’s primarily retards. After the falling knife I may pick a spot to buy some oil, but it really is a dead trade.” USO has more than doubled so far this year, while UCO has gained more than 145% so far in 2026. BATL shares have surged more than 58%, while XOM has gained by over 26% in the same time. For updates and corrections, email newsroom[at]stocktwits[dot]com. Retailers are still dealing with high shipping and supply chain costs, while heavy discounting and competitive pricing are putting more pressure on profit margins. The list released on Friday remains preliminary and will be finalized on June 18, ahead of the index reconstitution, which takes effect on June 29. The classification is significant because hundreds of institutional investors, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and mutual funds, base their portfolio allocations on these index classifications. As a result, any rebalancing can trigger large shifts in fund holdings, potentially triggering moves in the stocks in question. The Russell 1000 Index tracks the 1,000 largest publicly traded U.S. companies and represents the vast majority of the U.S. stock market’s total value, making it a key benchmark for large-cap investing. Nvidia has been excluding China from its forward guidance entirely since the H20 export restrictions. Any formal resumption of official sales would require analysts to rebuild a revenue line from a stated baseline of zero, Parekh said. He added that the re-rating wouldn’t be gradual, but immediate and considerably higher. "Having said that, I'm not expecting it," Parekh said. He added that Chinese AI companies have been establishing subsidiaries across Singapore, Malaysia, and other Asian markets where access to Nvidia compute is less restricted.
